title: The Mystery of the Missing Ribbon
markdown:
Oakhaven Primary’s Scarecrow Festival arrived the way it always did: straw, sunshine, and an allotment holding its breath. In the earthy hush of Mrs Gable’s shed she wrung her hands over an empty hook. Her garden rivalled half the village’s pride; her scones were spoken of in the careful tones reserved for miracles. Yesterday the Most Dapper Dandelion ribbon had hung there, sunshine-yellow satin meant for the scarecrow of sheer joy. Now only a faint circle marked the wood.

“Gone. Simply vanished.” Her voice, usually a comforting melody, had thinned to a thread.

Anya, twelve summers and scholarship-quiet, stood beside her. Under the unassuming cloak of her stillness a mind catalogued the world with a scribe’s ruthlessness. She had memorised every nail, cobweb, and speck in the shed. The missing ribbon was a discordant note. People called her clever girl in the tone that meant small. She carried that with a face that did not argue.

Finn arrived as if the scent of a problem had fetched him, a year younger and a universe more restless, bouncing on the balls of his feet. Under his jacket a bulky secret: a torch from their uncle’s garage, a beacon far above its station. “What’s all the fuss? Lost your homework again?”

“The ribbon,” Anya said, a low steady current in Mrs Gable’s worry. “Mrs Gable’s prize. It has vanished.”

Finn’s grin widened. A mystery. “Dibs on finding it.”

“It was not stolen. The shed was locked. The lock bears no tampering. My memory is quite precise.” She heard the defensive edge—years of well-meaning remarks—and hated it.

“Fine, fine, Professor Memory.” He was already turning toward the plots. “We’re not waiting for a clue to fall from the sky.”

The allotments, usually gentle industry, seemed to hold still. Damp soil. Crushed tomato leaves. Rows of beans made corridors. A late bee went home as if it had a rota. Finn swept the torch through tangled undergrowth, a silver dagger in the twilight, then through the shed again because he could not bear an unlit corner. In Mrs Gable’s doorway the beam made dust into a silent fleeting galaxy. Anya, usually anchored to the practical, watched it despite herself. She noted, because she noted everything, that the hook’s empty circle was the same diameter as the ribbon’s gathered knot. No one had torn it. Someone small had lifted it.

“See anything?” she whispered, kneeling by the foundation. Her eyes had found a minuscule scuff on a weathered plank, near a board that sat a little loose. A place a small careful thing might have scraped.

“Hold on.” Finn’s usual bounce quieted. He brought the light. The mark was far too small for a shoe, too delicate for a careless foot.

Anya pressed the board. It yielded on a dark opening no larger than a robin’s nest.

“Well, I’ll be,” Finn breathed. His hands, usually restless, went still.

They widened the entrance together, a shared effort that did not need a speech. Finn wanted to dive. Anya made him wait while she checked the board would not snap and bury a festival. A miniature pathway wound down into cool fragrant earth. Finn’s torch led, too bright, then shaded by his palm when the first pale root looked like a hand. Anya catalogued moss, root-shapes, and a faint sweet scent that grew with every step: honey and dew, the perfume of a hidden working. She counted her own breaths so she would not count the ways she might be wrong.

Then they saw them. Beings no taller than Anya’s thumb, bustling with earnest grace, clothes of gossamer and petal fragments. The Lintels: infinitesimal guardians of ordinary places. They coaxed dew into spheres, polished pebbles until they gleamed, and—Anya’s memory supplied the rest without being asked—charted the constellations visible through gaps in the soil.

A young Lintel held the ribbon, yellow satin against a form the size of a wish. Hair the colour of dandelion fluff. Eyes like polished dark stone. Anya’s memory offered a name as if it had always been filed there: Pip. He looked up at the two giants with fear and wonder mixed.

“He thought it was a fallen star,” said an elder Lintel, ancient as a fallen oak, voice like the rustle of dry leaves. “He collects celestial fragments for our autumn equinox. He meant no harm.”

Anya, who normally could not bear a thing out of place, felt a peculiar warmth. The mistake had been trying for wonder. “The ribbon is important,” she said, careful, a soft rumble in their world. “It’s for a festival. For Mrs Gable.”

Finn, to her quiet surprise, spoke next, boisterousness replaced by a thoughtful stillness that had only just arrived. “It’s all right, Pip. It looks a lot like a star. It has to go home.”

Pip, trembling a little, held the ribbon out. The Lintels nodded, solemn. “You must keep our secret,” the elder said. “The world is not ready for us. And we are not ready for the world.”

Anya and Finn exchanged a look. No vote required. They had found something more fragile than satin.

They came up into a thinner dark, dirt on knees, torch cooling in Finn’s hand. Anya folded the ribbon so the crease would not show. Finn did not ask to keep a petal souvenir. That, more than the descent, was how she knew he had understood.

Morning put the satin, slightly crumpled, back on Mrs Gable’s hook. She blamed a forgetful moment and cried the useful kind of tears. The scarecrows were judged; straw rustled in a gentle breeze; someone won Most Dapper and did not need to know why the ribbon looked as if it had travelled. Anya watched patches of earth and dew-kissed leaves as if they might still be working. Finn, for once, was content to observe, a silent partner in a thing they would not show. The hook held yellow again. Under the shed, the path they did not mention kept its own autumn, and the festival went on being only straw and sunshine to everyone else.
characters: Anya (quiet scholarship student with a ruthless memory who hates being underestimated), Finn (a cousin with a contraband torch and no patience)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic story for curious young teens
